## Overview

The [resistance vignette](Resistance.html) deploys a single drug and watches
resistance to it spread. In practice a programme has choices: which drug to use
first, whether to use several at once, and when to change. `magenta` can
represent three strategies, all configured through `drug_list_create()`:

* **multiple first line therapies (MFT)**, several drugs in use simultaneously,
  each patient receiving one at random
* **sequential cycling**, switching to the next drug once treatment failure
  passes a threshold
* **temporal cycling**, switching on a fixed schedule regardless of failure

This vignette also covers non-malarial fevers, which change how much drug
pressure a population experiences without changing the treatment policy at all.

```{r setup}
library(magenta)
```

---

## Deploying more than one drug

`drugs` takes a list, and `number_of_drugs` has to match its length. Drugs are
referred to by **zero indexed** position, so `drug_choice = 0` is the first drug
in the list.

```{r three-drugs}
drugs <- list(
  magenta:::drug_create_al(),
  magenta:::drug_create_asaq(),
  magenta:::drug_create_dhappq()
)
drug_names <- c("AL", "ASAQ", "DHA-PPQ")
```

Throughout this vignette we reuse a helper so that the only thing changing
between runs is the strategy:

```{r helpers}
loci <- c("crt 76T", "mdr1 86Y", "mdr1 184F", "mdr1 copy number",
          "kelch13 580Y", "plasmepsin 2-3 copy number")

strategy_list <- function(...) {
  drug_list_create(
    resistance_flag = TRUE,
    number_of_resistance_loci = 6,
    artemisinin_loci = 4,
    cost_of_resistance = rep(1, 6),
    drugs = drugs,
    number_of_drugs = 3,
    ...
  )
}

run_strategy <- function(drug_list, years = 20, seed = 1L) {
  pipeline(EIR = 10, N = 3000, years = years, ft = 0.4,
           num_loci = 6, plaf = rep(0.1, 6),
           update_length = 30, update_save = TRUE,
           human_update_save = TRUE, summary_saves_only = TRUE,
           genetics_df_without_summarising = TRUE,
           drug_list = drug_list, seed = seed)
}

# saved intervals, dropping the final element which is the simulation itself
saved <- function(out) out[seq_len(length(out) - 1)]

af_over_time <- function(out) {
  af <- do.call(rbind, lapply(saved(out), "[[", "af"))
  colnames(af) <- loci
  af
}

tf_over_time <- function(out) {
  unlist(lapply(saved(out), "[[", "overall_treatment_failure"))
}

# treatments given with each drug, per saved interval
usage_over_time <- function(out) {
  use <- do.call(rbind, lapply(saved(out), function(x) {
    x$succesfull_treatments + x$unsuccesful_treatments_lpf
  }))
  colnames(use) <- drug_names
  use
}
```

---

## Multiple first line therapies

With `mft_flag = TRUE`, each treated individual is given a drug drawn at random
according to `partner_drug_ratios`. Those ratios are the proportion of
treatments that use each drug, and must be the same length as `drugs`.

```{r mft}
out_mft <- run_strategy(
  strategy_list(mft_flag = TRUE, partner_drug_ratios = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3))
)

head(round(usage_over_time(out_mft), 1), 4)
```

All three drugs are in use at once, in roughly the requested proportions. An
unequal split is simply a different set of ratios, for example
`partner_drug_ratios = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)`.

Because each drug selects on a different set of loci, MFT spreads the selective
pressure out:

```{r mft-af}
plot_af <- function(af, main = "", legend_pos = "topleft") {
  years <- seq_len(nrow(af)) / 12
  matplot(years, af, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
          col = seq_len(ncol(af)), xlab = "Years", ylab = "Allele frequency",
          main = main)
  legend(legend_pos, legend = colnames(af), col = seq_len(ncol(af)),
         lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

plot_af(af_over_time(out_mft), main = "MFT, equal thirds")
```

Note that an individual's drug is cached for 15 days, so someone retreated
shortly after a failure receives the same drug rather than a fresh draw.

---

## Sequential cycling

With `sequential_cycling` set to a proportion, the model watches
`overall_treatment_failure` and moves to the next drug in the list once that
threshold is exceeded. `sequential_update` is the minimum number of years
between switches, which stops a noisy failure estimate causing repeated
changes.

```{r sequential}
out_seq <- run_strategy(
  strategy_list(mft_flag = FALSE,
                partner_drug_ratios = c(1, 0, 0),
                drug_choice = 0,
                sequential_cycling = 0.10,
                sequential_update = 3)
)
```

The messages record each switch. Plotting which drug is actually being used
makes the policy visible:

```{r sequential-usage, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_usage <- function(out, main = "") {
  use <- usage_over_time(out)
  years <- seq_len(nrow(use)) / 12
  matplot(years, use, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = seq_len(ncol(use)),
          xlab = "Years", ylab = "Treatments given", main = main)
  legend("topright", legend = colnames(use), col = seq_len(ncol(use)),
         lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
}

plot_usage(out_seq, main = "Sequential cycling at 10% treatment failure")
```

Three things about sequential cycling are easy to trip over.

1. The switch is evaluated in R **between update intervals**, inside
   `pipeline()`. It therefore only happens when `update_save = TRUE`.
2. It only happens when `resistance_flag` is `TRUE` for that year. If you stage
   resistance so that it is inactive during a burn-in, cycling is inactive then
   too.
3. It is skipped entirely when `mft_flag = TRUE`. MFT and cycling are
   alternatives, not features that combine.

The drug index wraps around, so after the last drug the policy returns to the
first.

---

## Temporal cycling

`temporal_cycling` switches drug every fixed number of years, whatever the
failure rate is doing. It cannot be combined with `sequential_cycling`;
`drug_list_create()` will stop if both are positive.

```{r temporal, fig.height = 4.5}
out_temporal <- run_strategy(
  strategy_list(mft_flag = FALSE,
                partner_drug_ratios = c(1, 0, 0),
                drug_choice = 0,
                temporal_cycling = 5)
)

plot_usage(out_temporal, main = "Temporal cycling every 5 years")
```

---

## Comparing strategies

Putting the three side by side on the same seed is the usual starting point for
a policy comparison. Here we hold everything else fixed and compare overall
treatment failure:

```{r compare, fig.height = 4.5}
out_single <- run_strategy(
  strategy_list(mft_flag = FALSE, partner_drug_ratios = c(0, 0, 1),
                drug_choice = 2)
)

tfs <- cbind(
  "DHA-PPQ only" = tf_over_time(out_single),
  "MFT"          = tf_over_time(out_mft),
  "Sequential"   = tf_over_time(out_seq),
  "Temporal"     = tf_over_time(out_temporal)
)

years <- seq_len(nrow(tfs)) / 12
matplot(years, tfs, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = seq_len(ncol(tfs)),
        xlab = "Years", ylab = "Overall treatment failure")
legend("topleft", legend = colnames(tfs), col = seq_len(ncol(tfs)),
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

A single run of a stochastic model is not a result. For anything you intend to
report, run many seeds per strategy and summarise the distribution; the
differences between strategies here are comparable in size to the variation
between seeds.

---

## Non-malarial fevers

Treatment coverage `ft` applies to clinical malaria. But in a real health
system, people are also treated for fevers that are not malaria, either because
no test was done or because a test was wrong. Those treatments still expose
parasites to the drug, and still put uninfected people into a prophylactic
state.

`nmf_list_create()` controls this. Like the drug constructors, it is currently
an internal function and so is called with `magenta:::`, even though
`pipeline()` documents it as the way to configure non-malarial fevers:

```{r nmf-list}
nmf <- magenta:::nmf_list_create(nmf_flag = TRUE, prob_of_testing_nmf = 0.5)
str(nmf[c("nmf_flag", "prob_of_testing_nmf")])
```

* `mean_nmf_frequency` is the mean number of days between non-malarial fevers,
  one value per age bracket, and `nmf_age_brackets` gives those brackets in
  days. The defaults are age specific and based on observed fever frequencies.
* `prob_of_testing_nmf` is the probability that a non-malarial fever is tested
  before antimalarials are given. Lowering it increases presumptive treatment.

Adding non-malarial fevers increases the amount of drug in circulation without
changing `ft`:

```{r nmf-run, fig.height = 4.5}
out_nmf <- pipeline(
  EIR = 10, N = 3000, years = 20, ft = 0.4,
  num_loci = 6, plaf = rep(0.1, 6),
  update_length = 30, update_save = TRUE,
  human_update_save = TRUE, summary_saves_only = TRUE,
  genetics_df_without_summarising = TRUE,
  drug_list = strategy_list(mft_flag = FALSE,
                            partner_drug_ratios = c(0, 0, 1),
                            drug_choice = 2),
  nmf_list = nmf,
  seed = 1L
)

ppq <- "plasmepsin 2-3 copy number"
years <- seq_len(nrow(af_over_time(out_single))) / 12
plot(years, af_over_time(out_single)[, ppq], type = "l", lwd = 2,
     col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Years", ylab = "Plasmepsin 2-3 frequency")
lines(years, af_over_time(out_nmf)[, ppq], lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft", legend = c("no non-malarial fevers", "with non-malarial fevers"),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

Whether this speeds resistance up or slows it down is not obvious in advance.
Extra treatment selects for resistance, but it also removes infections and
lengthens the population's time under prophylaxis, which reduces transmission.
That trade-off is one of the more interesting things the model can be used to
examine.

---

## Resistance beyond cure rates

Two further mechanisms change what resistance does, beyond the probability of
being cured.

**Slow parasite clearance.** If treatment succeeds but the individual is
carrying a strain resistant at any of the treating drug's `barcode_positions`,
they remain in the treated state for an extra `dur_SPC` days before moving to
prophylaxis, and keep only the resistant strains. This represents delayed
clearance, and gives resistant parasites a longer window in which to be
transmitted. Note that this is driven by the drug's own resistance positions,
not by `artemisinin_loci`.

**Gametocyte and oocyst effects.** `vector_adaptation_list_create()` holds
`gametocyte_sterilisation_flag`, `gametocyte_sterilisation` and
`oocyst_reduction_by_artemisinin`, which modify how well a recently treated host
infects mosquitoes. These are off by default. They are the natural place to
represent a transmission blocking drug, and are discussed in detail in the
[adding a new drug vignette](NewDrugs.html), which also notes a discrepancy
between the intent and the implementation that you should be aware of before
using them.
